claims.text: Coherent multilayer interfaces are the primary governor of time-dependent plastic-deformation resistance in HEA multilayer protective coatings.
High configurational entropy produces intrinsic lattice distortions in HEAs.
Coherent multilayer interfaces and intrinsic lattice distortions jointly pin dislocations strongly.
The proposed dislocation pinning elevates the activation energy for creep relative to a monolithic HEA coating.
Compositional differences between alternating HEA layers can produce lattice-parameter differences.
Coherent, misfit-stressed multilayer interfaces generate back-stresses.
Coherent interfacial boundaries disrupt dislocation-line continuity.
Misfit stresses at multilayer interfaces make the interfaces preferential dislocation-pinning sites.
The interfacial barrier increases the activation energy for dislocation nucleation.
The interfacial barrier increases the activation energy for dislocation glide.
Increasing the barriers to dislocation nucleation and glide reduces the rate of time-dependent plastic deformation.
Under identical stress and temperature, multilayer HEA coatings will have lower creep strain than monolithic HEA coatings.
Under identical stress and temperature, multilayer HEA coatings will exhibit a delayed onset of plastic deformation relative to monolithic HEA coatings.
The proposed resistance enhancement applies at moderate stresses and temperatures while the multilayer interfaces remain intact.
Interfacial degradation at very high temperature or extreme stress can diminish the resistance enhancement.
Interlayer thickness, layer-to-layer compositional differences, and coherent-interface stability can influence the extent of dislocation pinning.
A higher threshold for dislocation motion is equivalent to a higher activation energy for plastic deformation.
